issues.legal_issue: In an eviction proceeding, partial eviction must be assessed by objectively determining the landlord’s reasonable requirement and whether that requirement would be substantially satisfied by evicting the tenant from only part of the premises.
material_facts: The trial court assessed partial eviction in light of the landlord’s stated requirement, without applying the statutory test of reasonable requirement and substantial satisfaction.
The High Court accepted the trial court’s finding without addressing that test.
issues.conclusion: The courts must objectively determine the extent of the premises reasonably required and whether partial eviction would substantially satisfy that requirement; the matter was remanded for fresh consideration on the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 12(1)(c) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1977 requires the court, where the tenant agrees to remain in the rest of the building, to consider whether the landlord’s reasonable requirement would be substantially—not necessarily fully—satisfied by partial eviction. The requirement must be assessed objectively, not by the landlord’s mere desire or assertion.

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a landlord seeking eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.partial_occupation_would_substantially_s: The court determines that evicting the tenant from only part of the premises would substantially satisfy the landlord’s objectively assessed reasonable requirement.
predicates.tenant_agrees_to_remain_in_rest: The tenant agrees to continue occupying the remaining part of the premises.

issues.definition: When partial occupation would substantially satisfy the objectively assessed reasonable requirement and the tenant agrees to remain in the rest, the rule requires a decree for partial eviction.

issues.legal_issue: In a second appeal, a trial court’s factual finding obtained directly at the High Court’s request, without review by the intermediate appellate court, is not conclusive or immune from the High Court’s scrutiny.
material_facts: The matter was before the High Court in a second appeal.
The High Court had called directly on the trial court to make a finding on partial eviction, bypassing the District Judge, the last court on facts.
The High Court accepted the trial court’s finding without scrutinising it, although it had not been confirmed by the District Judge.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was required to scrutinise the trial court’s finding; it was not conclusive or immune from review. The appeal was allowed and the matter remanded to the High Court for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: A trial court finding directly obtained by the High Court, without the intermediate appellate court’s review, is not a conclusive finding of fact in a second appeal. The bypassed appellate review matters because the District Judge might have disagreed with the trial court; only if the District Judge agreed could the finding become binding on the High Court in second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.high_court_directly_requested_trial_cour: The High Court directly asked the trial court to make a factual finding.
predicates.intermediate_appellate_review_bypassed: The factual finding was not reviewed or confirmed by the intermediate appellate court.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when the High Court directly obtains a trial court finding without intermediate appellate review, it must scrutinise that finding.
